title: Two Birth Certificates and One Voice: Toulouse, the Abasto, and Medellin
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Valle Eden, the birth Uruguay claims
stops.date_confidence: Contested and rejected by the scholarly consensus. The date, place and parentage come from Gardel's own 1920 declaration at the Uruguayan consulate in Buenos Aires and from Uruguayan tradition (Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel', hipotesis uruguayista); no contemporary document from 1887 corroborates any part of it, and the Toulouse civil register of December 1890 contradicts it. Coordinates are those of Valle Eden per Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Valle Eden' (31 49 24 S, 56 10 38 O); the claimed birth site is the nearby estancia Santa Blanca. This stop records the claim, not a fact.
stops.campa: A day's ride from Tacuarembo, in a valley of low stone hills, stands the estancia Santa Blanca. Uruguay holds that a boy was born here on the eleventh of December 1887 to Carlos and Maria Gardel, and that the boy is the singer. No paper from 1887 says so. The claim rests entirely on what the man himself swore in a consulate in Buenos Aires thirty-three years later, with no documents in his hand and nothing to check the statement against. Two republics will spend the following century arguing over a birth certificate that neither of them can produce.
suggested_refs: The Museo Carlos Gardel at Valle Eden, inaugurated 11 December 1999, on Gardel's own birthday
Erasmo Silva Cabrera's 1967 book, founding text of the uruguayista account

stops.name: Toulouse, the register at La Grave
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the French civil register of Toulouse and carried by both the English and Spanish Wikipedia articles as the consensus birth record. Coordinates are those of the Hopital de La Grave per Wikipedia (French), 'Hopital de La Grave' (43 36 03 N, 1 26 03 E). The register itself was not fetched in this pass; it reaches this file through the two encyclopaedia articles and through the genealogists Ruffie and Galopa as they cite it.
stops.campa: In the hospice of La Grave on the left bank of the Garonne, a ward kept for the poor and for unmarried women, Berthe Gardes is delivered of a son. She is twenty-five and works as a laundress. The clerk enters the child in the French civil register as Charles Romuald Gardes, and where the father's name belongs he writes that it is unknown. Every genealogist who has gone looking for the singer's origin has come back to this page; it is the earliest document in the whole case. The midwife Jenny Bazin signs as witness.
suggested_refs: The Toulouse civil birth register entry for Charles Romuald Gardes, 11 December 1890
The 1983 monument by Martha Baez and Norberto Perlmutter in the Jardins Compans-Caffarelli, Toulouse

stops.name: Toulouse, the recognition that was never made official
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel'. The place at which the statement was signed is not given by that source; the pin is the Toulouse city centre coordinate rather than a located address. The quote carried on this stop was spoken in Buenos Aires years afterward and is placed here for its subject; it reaches the file only through Wikipedia's citation of Collier (1986), p. 7, the book itself not having been fetched.
stops.campa: Eleven days after the delivery Berthe Gardes signs a statement naming Paul Laserre, a married man, as the father of her child. The recognition is never made official. Nothing changes on the register, where the father remains unknown, and she keeps the boy, the surname Gardes and no maintenance from anyone. Laserre stays in Toulouse and drops out of the record entirely. Years afterward, in Buenos Aires, his mother asks the son whether he would like to see the man.
stops.quote: I don't even wish to see him.
stops.quote_source: Carlos Gardel on his biological father, spoken to his mother in Buenos Aires, quoted in Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel', citing Simon Collier (1986), p. 7
suggested_refs: Simon Collier, The Life, Music and Times of Carlos Gardel (1986)

stops.name: Bordeaux, the steamer Don Pedro
stops.date_confidence: The year and the ship are attested by Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel'; no month or day of departure is given by any source consulted, so both default to 01. The departure month is bounded only by the March 1893 arrival in Buenos Aires.
stops.campa: Berthe Gardes takes ship at Bordeaux with a boy of two, aboard the steamer Don Pedro, bound for the Rio de la Plata. She travels the way thousands of French and Italian women travel in these years, toward a city that is doubling every decade and is short of hands to wash and press its linen. He will not see France again for thirty years, and when he does he will come back to it by way of Madrid. Nothing in the record marks the child out from any other child in steerage.
suggested_refs: Passenger records of the SS Don Pedro, Bordeaux to Buenos Aires, 1893

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the boy comes off the boat
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction between sources, not resolved here. Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel' gives 11 March 1893; Wikipedia (French), 'Carlos Gardel' states that Argentine documents attest the arrival of Berthe Gardes and her son Charles on 9 March 1893. The month and year are secure, the day is not. Coordinates are those of the Darsena Norte rather than a specific berth.
stops.campa: The Don Pedro ties up in the darsena and the boy walks into Buenos Aires under the name Charles Gardes. Argentine papers record the arrival of mother and son; the day they record is not agreed, the ninth of March in one account and the eleventh in another. Berthe is twenty-seven and has no husband. The register that names her son and refuses to name his father is four thousand leagues behind her. She takes work as a laundress and presser in the French style on Calle Montevideo, and a room a few blocks off on Calle Uruguay.
suggested_refs: Argentine immigration records for Berthe Gardes and Charles Gardes, March 1893

segments.name: The Laundress's Son in San Nicolas

stops.name: Calle Uruguay 162, the two-person household
stops.date_confidence: The address and the years of residence (1893 to about 1904) are attested by Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel'; the month here is an ordering device only. Coordinates are corrected: the research pool carried a positive latitude, which places the point in the North Atlantic. Calle Uruguay 162 in San Nicolas sits near 34 36 S, 58 22 W.
stops.campa: The room is in San Nicolas, close enough to the port to hear it and a few blocks from the theatres of Calle Corrientes. Berthe irons other people's linen. The boy grows up bilingual without anyone deciding that he should, French at the washtub and Spanish in the street, and the neighbours settle on Carlitos. He is a foreigner's son in a city where nearly every child is a foreigner's son, and nobody in the street remarks on it. The household is two people and it stays two people for the next forty years.
suggested_refs: The laundry premises on Calle Montevideo where Berthe Gardes worked

stops.name: Almagro, the Salesians of Colegio Pio IX
stops.date_confidence: The schooling is attested by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel' for 1901; month and day default to 01. The coordinate is approximate and unverified: the Spanish Wikipedia article titled 'Colegio Pio IX' describes the Montevideo school, not the Buenos Aires one, and cannot be used as a cite for this pin. The Buenos Aires Colegio Salesiano Pio IX adjoins the Basilica de Maria Auxiliadora y San Carlos in Almagro; this coordinate is that neighbourhood, pending a Buenos Aires source. Note also that the whole schooling episode falls inside the disputed years: the uruguayista account places him in Montevideo instead.
stops.campa: The Salesians take him in at their school in Almagro, beside the basilica of Maria Auxiliadora, where the priests run classes, workshops and a choir on Don Bosco's system: trades in the morning, discipline all day, singing as an ordinary part of the timetable. He does not stay long. Formal schooling ends here and the education that replaces it happens in the wings of theatres and across the counter of a cafe. Whether he was ever in this building at all depends on which of his two birth certificates is believed.
suggested_refs: Registers of the Colegio Salesiano Pio IX, Almagro, Buenos Aires, for 1901 and 1902

stops.name: Teatro Opera, the claque and the wings
stops.date_confidence: Biographical tradition rather than document. Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel' places the claque work under a figure known as Patasanta around 1900 and the stagehand job at the Teatro Opera in 1902, and does not source either as an attested fact. Coordinates from Wikipedia (English), 'Teatro Opera' for Avenida Corrientes 860. The quote is Gardel's own recollection given in 1933, thirty-one years after the events it describes.
stops.campa: He gets work in the theatres of Calle Corrientes: leading the claque for a man remembered only as Patasanta, clapping on cue for a fee, and then shifting scenery at the Teatro Opera on Avenida Corrientes. This is the only conservatory he ever enters, and he pays for it by moving flats and by applauding on command for singers who have names. From the wings he watches Titta Ruffo and Emilio Sagi Barba, and hears how an operatic baritone reaches the back of a house without ever shouting at it.
stops.quote: Esos fueron mis primeros conocimientos artisticos y asi fue como consegui obtener aquella voz blanca con la cual me di a conocer.
stops.quote_source: Carlos Gardel, interviewed in revista Antena (Buenos Aires), 18 March 1933, cited in Osvaldo Barsky and Julian Barsky, Gardel, la biografia (Taurus, 2004), p. 89
suggested_refs: Revista Antena (Buenos Aires), 18 March 1933, the interview in which Gardel describes his theatre apprenticeship
sources: Barsky and Barsky, Gardel, la biografia (2004)

stops.name: Abasto, singing at the O'Rondeman
stops.date_confidence: Traditional. Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel' locates the cafe at Aguero and Humahuaca and places Gardel's singing there in the second half of the 1900s without a firm year; the date given here is an ordering device inside that span. Coordinates are corrected: the pool carried a positive latitude and a longitude some 450 metres west of the corner.
stops.campa: At the corner of Aguero and Humahuaca, a few steps from the great Abasto produce market, the O'Rondeman is a cafe of carters, drovers and market men. Gardel sings criolla and payada there for whatever the room decides to give him. The Abasto is his territory now, and the name the neighbourhood hands him, El Morocho del Abasto, the dark-haired boy from the market, stays on his billing for the rest of his working life. The repertoire is all country song. There is no tango in it yet.
suggested_refs: The site of the Cafe O'Rondeman at Aguero and Humahuaca, Abasto

stops.name: Guardia Vieja, the meeting with Razzano
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction resting on a single retrospective testimony. Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel' notes that the year 1911 is placed there by Razzano himself in his memoirs, not by any document, and that the memoirs put the encounter in a friend's house on Guardia Vieja a few metres from the Abasto market. The block of Guardia Vieja between Jean Jaures and Anchorena was renamed Pasaje Carlos Gardel long after the fact; identifying it as the exact spot is local tradition. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: In a friend's house on Guardia Vieja, a few metres from the Abasto market, he meets Jose Razzano, a Uruguayan of about his own age with a voice that sits above his own. They sing against each other, then with each other, and then stop singing against each other for good. The block between Jean Jaures and Anchorena will be renamed Pasaje Carlos Gardel long afterward. Razzano is the only person who ever put a year to this meeting, and he put it there from memory, in a book of his own, decades after the front room.
suggested_refs: Jose Razzano's memoirs, sole source for the 1911 dating of the meeting

stops.name: Casa Tagini, the first records
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel': the Columbia contract through Casa Tagini falls in 1912 and the discs are issued in 1913. Month and day default to 01. The coordinate is corrected for hemisphere and is approximate; no street address for the Casa Tagini premises is given by the source.
stops.campa: Casa Tagini, agent in Buenos Aires for Columbia, puts him in front of a recording horn: seven double-sided discs of criollo material, among them Pobre mi madre querida. He is twenty-one by one certificate and twenty-four by the other. There is no microphone in the room. The voice has to be aimed into a brass cone and driven hard enough to cut wax, which favours singers who push and punishes singers who breathe. The records are issued the following year under his own name.
suggested_refs: The seven Columbia double-sided discs of 1912, issued 1913

stops.name: Armenonville, the first paid engagement
stops.date_confidence: The date is disputed inside one source family and is left unresolved. Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel' gives 14 June 1914 for the duo debut; Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Armenonville' states the pair performed there at a New Year party on 1 January 1914. The figure of 70 pesos a night, carried by the research pool, is uncited in either article and is not asserted here. Coordinates corrected: the Armenonville stood on Avenida Alvear in Recoleta, roughly where the Automovil Club Argentino now is, not in Palermo.
stops.campa: The Armenonville stands on Avenida Alvear in Recoleta, a cabaret with a garden, patronised by men who arrive in motorcars. Gardel and Razzano are engaged there, and it is the first work either of them is paid properly for. From the cabaret they move onto the stage of the Teatro Nacional on Corrientes inside the same twelve months. The date of the debut itself is not settled: one account gives the fourteenth of June, another a New Year party on the first of January.
suggested_refs: The Armenonville cabaret on Avenida Alvear, demolished in 1926
The Teatro Nacional at Corrientes 960

stops.name: Montevideo, the Teatro Royal
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel'. Coordinates corrected for hemisphere: the pool's positive latitude placed the theatre in the mid-Atlantic.
stops.campa: The duo crosses the Plata and opens at the Teatro Royal in Montevideo on the eighteenth of June. Razzano is Uruguayan and coming home. Gardel is arriving for the first time as a working performer in the city whose consulate will, five years from now, issue him a nationality on his word alone. Montevideo takes to the pair the way Buenos Aires already has. The house is theirs from the first night, and the run is a success on the scale that gets reported back across the river.
suggested_refs: The Teatro Royal, Montevideo, and the June 1915 season

stops.name: Teatro San Martin, Juan Moreira on the stage
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel'. Coordinates corrected for hemisphere; the theatre stood at Corrientes 1530. The same year's tour of Brazil, which the pool assigns to two different companies in two different entries (Compania Dramatica Rioplatense in one, Elias Alippi's company in the other) and for which no venue is named by any source, is left out of this file rather than staged at a theatre nobody places him in.
stops.campa: On the stage of the Teatro San Martin at Corrientes 1530, Gardel appears in a staging of Juan Moreira, the gaucho outlaw drama that has been the standing spectacle of the Rio de la Plata for thirty years. He is a singer placed inside a play rather than an actor, which is how the cinema will use him too. The costume is poncho and boots and the whole gaucho apparatus, worn in a city that has not needed any of it for a generation. Paris will demand the same of him thirteen years from now.
suggested_refs: The Juan Moreira drama, staple of the Rio de la Plata stage since the 1880s

stops.name: Buenos Aires, shot in the street
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel', which gives no street, no assailant, no cause and no account of the recovery. The pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate because the location of the altercation is a gap in the record, not because it is known.
stops.campa: In December he is shot and wounded in a street altercation in Buenos Aires. He is twenty-five by one register and twenty-eight by the other, and his name has begun to be worth money to other people. Whatever happened that night interrupts nothing; he is back at work. The sources consulted name no street, no assailant and no cause, and give no account of the recovery beyond the bare fact that there was one. Whether anybody was ever charged, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires police and press notices of December 1915, unlocated in this pass

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the tango learns to be sung
stops.date_confidence: The year, the composers and the figure of roughly ten thousand copies are attested by Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel', and the ten-thousand figure is independently corroborated inside this corpus by max_glucksmann.journey.json. Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Mi noche triste' specifies Jose Ricardo on guitar and the Disco Gardel-Razzano imprint, later Odeon: Gardel-Razzano is the billing, the sung voice is Gardel's alone. Month and day default to 01. The coordinate is a microcentro approximation, not a located address for Glucksmann's premises.
stops.campa: Pascual Contursi has put words to a tango of Samuel Castriota that had none, a man alone in a room addressing the furniture a woman left behind. Gardel sings it with Jose Ricardo on guitar, and the disc goes out on the Gardel-Razzano imprint belonging to Max Glucksmann's house, later Odeon. Before this record the tango is a thing danced; after it the tango is a thing sung, by one person, about one loss. It sells on the order of ten thousand copies.
suggested_refs: Carlos Gardel, 'Mi noche triste' (1917), music by Samuel Castriota, words by Pascual Contursi, guitar by Jose Ricardo

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Villoldo's song on a Gardel record
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year only, through angel_villoldo.journey.json citing Wikipedia (English), 'Angel Villoldo'; month and day default to 01, and the recording location is presumed Buenos Aires rather than stated. The relation is one-directional and musical: no meeting, letter or photograph connects the two men. Pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate, inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: Cantar eterno goes onto a Gardel and Razzano record. The song belongs to Angel Villoldo, who wrote the first tangos anyone thought to buy and who has two years left to live. No meeting between the two men is on record, no letter, no photograph. What passes between them is a piece of paper with notes on it, going from the man who invented the trade to the man who is about to become its face. Villoldo dies in 1919. Gardel goes on singing his material for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The 1917 Gardel-Razzano recording of Angel Villoldo's 'Cantar eterno'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a silent film for a singer
stops.date_confidence: The premiere date is attested by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel'. The director is Francisco Defilippis Novoa per Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Flor de durazno'; the research pool's parenthetical naming a Julio or Jose as director is wrong and is dropped, as is its claim that Razzano was involved, which that article does not support. The cinema at which it premiered is not named by the sources consulted, so the pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate.
stops.campa: Flor de durazno opens in Buenos Aires on the twenty-eighth of September, directed by Francisco Defilippis Novoa, with Gardel in it. Which cinema showed it first, the sources consulted do not name. The picture does not succeed, and he stays away from cameras for thirteen years, by which time the camera has learned to listen. The film is silent. He is heavy, he is uneasy in front of the lens, and the one instrument he possesses cannot be used at all: an audience that has come to hear him sits in a dark room and watches him mouth.
suggested_refs: Flor de durazno (1917), dir. Francisco Defilippis Novoa, Gardel's film debut

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Isabel del Valle
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel' gives the meeting at the Esmeralda theatre, her age of fourteen and a relationship of more than a decade; the account rests on later testimony rather than on contemporary document, and no month or day is given, so both default to 01. The Esmeralda theatre is not located by any source consulted, so the pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate.
stops.campa: He meets Isabel del Valle at the Esmeralda theatre. Where that theatre stood, no source consulted says. She is fourteen; he is thirty by the French register. The relationship runs for more than a decade and both of them keep it out of the papers: no marriage, no public appearance, no photograph offered to anybody. In everything the public is given about him, the only woman in his life is his mother. What survives of the other one is testimony given long afterward, not document.
suggested_refs: Later testimony of Isabel del Valle, principal source for the relationship

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the word sworn at the Uruguayan consulate
stops.date_confidence: The act is attested only in bare form: Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel' says that in 1920 he applied to the Uruguayan consulate in Buenos Aires for a certificate of nationality and an identity card. It gives no month, no folio and no witnesses; the witness names Juan Lagisquet and Jose Razzano, which the research pool carried, appear in no source fetched here and are dropped. The month above is an ordering device. The consulate address is not attested, so the pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate.
stops.campa: He walks into the Uruguayan consulate in Buenos Aires without papers and swears that he was born at Tacuarembo on the eleventh of December 1887, son of Carlos and Maria Gardel, both Uruguayans. Nothing is verified, because there is nothing to verify it against; the act consists entirely of one man's word about himself, taken down and stamped. The consulate issues the certificate. His nationality and his first identity card both come out of this one sheet of paper.
suggested_refs: The 1920 Uruguayan certificate of nationality, cornerstone of the uruguayista case

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first legitimate identity card
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel', which dates 4 October 1920 to his first legitimate identity document, an Argentine cedula obtained on the strength of the Uruguayan certification. The research pool conflated the two documents by describing this one as listing him as Uruguayan; they are separate papers issued by separate states and are separated here. Pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate, no office address being attested.
stops.campa: On the strength of the Uruguayan certificate the Argentine authorities issue him a cedula on the fourth of October, the first legitimate identity document he has ever held. He is thirty years old and has lived in this country since he was two without any papers at all, working, recording and touring on nothing. The card is Argentine. The nationality behind it is Uruguayan. The register that recorded his birth is French, and it sits in a municipal archive in Toulouse.
suggested_refs: Gardel's Argentine cedula de identidad, 4 October 1920

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the oath of Argentine citizenship
stops.date_confidence: Both dates are attested by Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel': the application on 7 March 1923 and the oath on 1 May 1923. That article also carries the historians' reading that the timing was driven partly by a wish to avoid French conscription obligations ahead of a planned tour of France; the motive is an interpretation, not a documented statement of Gardel's. Pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate.
stops.campa: He applies for Argentine citizenship on the seventh of March and takes the oath on the first of May. He is now a naturalised Argentine who acquired his previous nationality by declaration and was registered at birth in a third country. Historians tie the timing to a tour of France already being planned, and to the military service a Frenchman born in 1890 still owes the French state; an Argentine passport makes that question disappear. The motive is their reading, not anything he is recorded as saying.
suggested_refs: Gardel's Argentine naturalisation file, 7 March to 1 May 1923

segments.name: Madrid, Barcelona, and the End of the Duo

stops.name: Madrid, the Teatro Apolo
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel'. The run of some forty performances is given by the same source. The theatre on the Calle de Alcala was demolished in 1929; the coordinate is its site.
stops.campa: The duo opens in Europe at the Teatro Apolo on the Calle de Alcala. Madrid has heard tangos played. It has not heard them sung like this. The pair arrive billed as an Argentine act and are received as one, which settles the nationality question for a paying audience even while it stays wide open in the archives. Gardel is thirty-three and outside the Americas for the first time since a steamer carried him into them at two years old. The run goes to some forty performances.
suggested_refs: The Teatro Apolo, Calle de Alcala, Madrid, demolished 1929

stops.name: Toulouse, meeting the Gardes family
stops.date_confidence: Attested by both Wikipedia (Spanish) and Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel', which place the visit during the Spanish tour of 1923 to 1924 without a month or a day; both default to 01 and the year is chosen as the later of the two. Pin is the Toulouse city coordinate, no address for the relatives being given.
stops.campa: He goes north to Toulouse and meets the Gardes family, his mother's people, thirty-one years after Berthe carried him out of France. There is a hospice on the Garonne with his birth entered in its register and an empty column where a father should be, and there are cousins in this town who know exactly who he is and where he came from. He goes back to the stage afterward, keeps the Uruguayan certificate in his pocket, and tells the press what he has always told the press. What is said in that house nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The Gardes relatives of Toulouse, visited during the 1923-1924 European tour

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the duo comes apart
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the month by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel', which gives the cause as a laryngeal injury ending Razzano's singing voice and his move to managing Gardel; the day is not given and defaults to 01. Pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate.
stops.campa: Razzano's larynx fails. The upper voice that made a duo a duo is gone and does not come back, and the partnership formed in a front room on Guardia Vieja fourteen years earlier ends as a singing arrangement. Everything that carries Gardel's name beyond the Rio de la Plata happens after this, and he does all of it alone. Razzano becomes his manager, which keeps the two men in business with each other for years yet, on paper rather than on a stage.
suggested_refs: Jose Razzano's move from partner to manager, September 1925

stops.name: Barcelona, the solo debut at the Teatro Goya
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel'. Coordinates corrected: Wikipedia (Catalan), 'Teatre Goya (Barcelona)' gives the address as Carrer de Joaquin Costa 68-72 in El Raval, Ciutat Vella, some 2.4 km from the Gracia coordinate the research pool carried. The theatre opened on 30 September 1916, which is consistent with a 1925 run.
stops.campa: His first tour as a solo act opens on the tenth of November at the Teatro Goya on Carrer de Joaquin Costa in the Raval, in a house barely nine years old, built in 1916. The run is long and it works, and Barcelona keeps him for months. Spain has now heard him twice, once as half of something and once whole. Without Razzano beside him the material shifts: fewer duets, more tango, and a delivery built around one man standing still at the front of a stage with a guitar behind him.
suggested_refs: The Teatre Goya, Carrer de Joaquin Costa 68-72, El Raval, Barcelona

stops.name: Barcelona, singing into a microphone
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the studio. Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel' attests that Gardel began electrical recording in Barcelona in 1926; the identification of the Casa Odeon studio and its coordinate are inferred rather than stated by that source, and month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: In Barcelona he sings into an electrical microphone for the first time. The horn that punished breathing is finished. What the microphone hears is the thing he owns that no brass cone could ever carry: the small catch at the end of a line, the half-spoken word, the sound of a man deliberately not raising his voice. The records made from here on are a different instrument from the ones cut into wax at Casa Tagini in 1912. Which studio he stood in, the source does not name.
suggested_refs: Gardel's first electrical recordings, Barcelona, 1926

stops.name: Abasto, the house at Jean Jaures 735
stops.date_confidence: The purchase year is attested by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel'; month and day default to 01. Coordinates from Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Museo Casa Carlos Gardel' (34 36 06 S, 58 24 28 O), correcting both the hemisphere error and a longitude some 850 metres off in the research pool.
stops.campa: He buys a house at Jean Jaures 735, in the Abasto, and installs his mother in it. Berthe Gardes has been ironing other people's linen in Buenos Aires for thirty-four years and is done with it. From the corner where he sang for carters at the O'Rondeman to the front door of this house is a walk of three blocks, and it has taken him roughly twenty years to cover them. He lives here himself until 1933, comes and goes between tours, and keeps the address to the end of his life.
suggested_refs: The house at Jean Jaures 735, Abasto, later the Museo Casa Carlos Gardel

stops.name: Theatre Femina, the gala before the debut
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel', which describes the appearance as a charity gala preceding the official Paris debut. The coordinate is that of the Theatre Femina on the Champs-Elysees.
stops.campa: Paris hears him first on the thirtieth of September, at a charity gala in the Theatre Femina on the Champs-Elysees, an informal appearance two days ahead of the engagement that counts. The tango is already fashionable in this city; what the fashion has not yet been supplied with is a singer. The country about to adopt him is the one that entered his birth in a register and then lost track of him for thirty-five years. He is thirty-seven and speaks almost no French.
suggested_refs: The Theatre Femina, Champs-Elysees, and the gala of 30 September 1928

stops.name: Montmartre, the cabaret Florida
stops.date_confidence: The date and venue are attested by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel'. The figure of seventy thousand records sold in three months is carried by Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel' as a report rather than an audited number, and is given here as the count that circulates.
stops.campa: The cabaret Florida in Montmartre is where the Paris engagement properly begins, and the city takes him at once. The press writes him up. The records move, seventy thousand of them in three months by the figure that circulates, which nobody has audited. He is a Frenchman by register, an Argentine by oath and a Uruguayan on paper. To sing tangos in this room he has to appear as a gaucho, in poncho and boots, because that is what the fashion requires an Argentine to look like.
suggested_refs: The cabaret Florida, Montmartre, October 1928

stops.name: Paris, the letter to Razzano from the Rue Fontaine
stops.date_confidence: The letter carries no date; c.1928 is the estimate given by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel', which quotes the text at note 44 under the internal reference CartaGardelRazzano and gives no archival repository for the original. The month above is an ordering device only. The text was read verbatim on that page; the original document was not seen. Pin is the canonical Paris coordinate, the letter having been written somewhere in the city.
stops.campa: He writes to Razzano about El Garron on the Rue Fontaine, a basement full of French, Americans and Japanese paying serious money to sit inside a fashion. He sets it against the Armenonville of fourteen years earlier, where the room was made of people like himself who felt the tango as he felt it, and he does not flatter the comparison. The letter carries no date and is placed at 1928 by estimate. Where the original is kept, the source that carries the text does not say.
stops.quote: Mi viejo y querido Pepe: Ayer estuve dos horas, entre copas, charlas y jarana, en «El Garron» de la Rue Fontaine. Es un bodegon como los del Once, ni mas ni menos. Pero en estos dias se llena de franchutes, de americanos, hasta de japoneses, con un cargamento impresionante de plata. La fiebre del tango los lleva alli. Yo me acordaba de aquel debut del duo Gardel-Razzano, en el viejo «Armenonville»... ¿Te acordas del julepe que tenia? Ahora aqui, convertido de repente en un señor, me doy cuenta de que, con todas las fulerias que pasamos, en el viejo «Armenonville» estabamos entre gente igual a nosotros, que sentian el tango tanto como nosotros mismos. Aqui, en cambio, el gotan es una moda pasajera y caprichosa como todas. Enterate: para cantar tangos, hay que vestirse de gaucho.
stops.quote_source: Letter from Carlos Gardel to Jose Razzano, written from Paris, c. 1928, quoted in Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel', note 44
suggested_refs: The cabaret El Garron, Rue Fontaine, Montmartre, centre of the Paris tango trade

stops.name: Palais Garnier, the Bal des Petits Lits Blancs
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the year by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel'; no month or day is given and both default to 01. A separate claim in the research pool that Gardel gave concerts at the Opera Garnier across 1928 and 1929 came from the dossier alone and could not be verified against a fetched source; only the charity gala is carried here.
stops.campa: He sings at the Bal des Petits Lits Blancs inside the Palais Garnier, the charity gala of the Paris season, in a house built for grand opera. The invitation comes from the room where the season's fashions are decided rather than the room where they are bought, from people with no notion of where the Abasto is or what is sold there. Some twenty-seven years earlier he was being paid to lead the applause for other men in a theatre on Corrientes. The gaucho costume goes on again.
suggested_refs: The Bal des Petits Lits Blancs, annual charity gala at the Palais Garnier

stops.name: Buenos Aires, home after fifteen months
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel'. Pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate; no dock or reception venue is named by the source.
stops.campa: He comes home to Buenos Aires after fifteen months away. The city that let a market singer go to Europe takes back a man who has sold records in France by the tens of thousands and who now belongs, in a way nobody has yet found the words for, to the whole Rio de la Plata rather than to any one neighbourhood in it. There are six years left, and almost everything anybody now knows him for is still ahead of him. His mother is in the house at Jean Jaures.
suggested_refs: Press coverage of Gardel's return to Buenos Aires, 16 June 1929

stops.name: Avenida Santa Fe, the voice goes on the air
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by max_glucksmann.journey.json, which places Gardel's radio debut on Radio Splendid, broadcasting from inside the Grand Splendid theatre on Avenida Santa Fe, on 1 October 1929. Pin inherited unchanged from that file.
stops.campa: He makes his radio debut from Radio Splendid, the station Max Glucksmann has installed inside his own Grand Splendid theatre on Avenida Santa Fe, in the same building where Gardel cuts his Odeon records and sings from the stage. Four weeks later the New York market collapses and the record trade that carried him this far begins to contract. The voice now leaves the building without needing a disc to travel in, and anyone with a receiver and no gramophone at all can have him in the room.
suggested_refs: Radio Splendid, broadcasting from the Grand Splendid theatre, Avenida Santa Fe

stops.name: Buenos Aires, fifteen shorts for Eduardo Morera
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel', which also gives 3 May 1931 for the premiere of the shorts at the Cine Astral. No studio address is named for the filming, so the pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate.
stops.campa: Eduardo Morera puts him in front of a camera that can hear, and they shoot fifteen short sound films in Buenos Aires: Gardel singing, mostly, with the occasional spoken introduction between numbers. Thirteen years after the silent Flor de durazno the technology has finally caught up with the only asset he has. They are among the earliest Argentine ventures into sound cinema. The shorts premiere at the Cine Astral the following May, by which time he is in France.
suggested_refs: The fifteen Eduardo Morera shorts of 1930, premiered at the Cine Astral, 3 May 1931

stops.name: Nice, the Riviera months and a written contradiction
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the venue and approximate as to the pin. Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel' has him leaving for France in January 1931 and reaching Paris to film for Paramount only at the end of April, the intervening months spent on the Riviera; it mentions Nice appearances but does not name the Casino de la Jetee-Promenade as the venue, and no page for that pier could be reached to check the coordinate, which reads as somewhat too far east. The same article frames the dismissal of guitarist Jose Aguilar as provoked by a homophobic remark against Gardel. The 1931 witnessed declaration is attested by Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel' citing Eliseo Alvarez (1995), without a stated place of signature.
stops.campa: He spends the first months of the year on the Riviera, appearing at Nice, while Paramount gets ready for him. Here he dismisses the guitarist Jose Aguilar from the ensemble after a remark made against him. Here too, inside the same year, he writes down and has witnessed a version of his origin that flatly contradicts the certificate he swore to in a Buenos Aires consulate eleven years earlier. The witnessed document gives the Toulouse date and names Berthe Gardes as his mother.
stops.quote: I am French, born in Toulouse, 11 December 1890, son of Berthe Gardes.
stops.quote_source: Carlos Gardel, witnessed document of 1931, quoted in Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel', citing Eliseo Alvarez, Carlos Gardel: biografia autorizada (De la Urraca, 1995)
suggested_refs: The 1931 witnessed declaration of French birth, cited by Alvarez (1995)

stops.name: Joinville-le-Pont, the Paramount factory on the Marne
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel' places his arrival in Paris to film for Paramount at Joinville at the end of April 1931; the day defaults to 01. Coordinates from Wikipedia (French), 'Studios de Joinville', 20 avenue du General-Gallieni (48 49 10 N, 2 28 16 E), correcting a pin some 1.3 km off in the research pool. The four Joinville features belong to 1931 and 1932; the research pool's range of 1931 to 1934 is wrong, the later films being American.
stops.campa: Paramount's European studio at Joinville-le-Pont on the Marne is a factory for shooting the same picture in six languages, and Gardel is hired to carry the Spanish end of it. He reaches Paris for the work at the end of April. The suburb is a short ride from the Rue Fontaine basement he described to Razzano. He acts adequately and he sings extremely well, and the studio builds the films around that proportion. Las luces de Buenos Aires is made here, then Esperame, then La casa es seria.
suggested_refs: Paramount's Joinville-le-Pont studios, 20 avenue du General-Gallieni

stops.name: Joinville-le-Pont, Le Pera and Mi Buenos Aires querido
stops.date_confidence: The Le Pera collaboration is attested by Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel'; Melodia de arrabal, which carries Mi Buenos Aires querido, is a Joinville production of 1932. Month and day default to 01. The research pool folded the Joinville and New York studio periods into a single 1934 entry placed at 'New York and Paris'; they are separated here, Mi Buenos Aires querido belonging to Joinville and Por una cabeza to the later American films.
stops.campa: Alfredo Le Pera, an Argentine writer brought into the Paramount operation, starts writing for him, and the songs go on being sung after the films they were built to sit inside have stopped being shown. From here to the end, Le Pera writes the words to nearly everything Gardel sings, and the two of them work almost exclusively on each other. Melodia de arrabal is shot at Joinville and carries Mi Buenos Aires querido, a homesick tango written on the Marne about a city on the Plata.
suggested_refs: Melodia de arrabal (1932), Paramount Joinville, carrying 'Mi Buenos Aires querido'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, telling the press again where he is from
stops.date_confidence: The quote is dated to 25 October 1933 and attributed to El Telegrafo of Paysandu, Uruguay, by Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel', citing Collier (1986), p. 72; Collier was not fetched. No source consulted places Gardel physically in Paysandu on that day, so he is not staged there: the pin is his own canonical Buenos Aires base. A similar statement attributed to La Tribuna Popular of Buenos Aires in the same year could not be confirmed, and whether the two press citations record one utterance or two is unresolved.
stops.campa: Asked once more where he comes from, he answers as he has answered since 1920. The line runs in the Uruguayan press in October and versions of it circulate on the Buenos Aires side of the river too. He is by now the most famous man in the Rio de la Plata and among the least documented, holding an Argentine passport obtained through a Uruguayan certificate obtained through nothing but his own sworn word. He does not correct it in public. In November he sails for New York.
stops.quote_source: Carlos Gardel, quoted in El Telegrafo (Paysandu, Uruguay), 25 October 1933, cited in Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel', citing Simon Collier (1986), p. 72
suggested_refs: El Telegrafo (Paysandu), 25 October 1933

stops.name: Astoria, Queens, the four American pictures
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Wikipedia (English), 'Kaufman Astoria Studios': all the films starring Gardel made in the United States were shot at Astoria Studios. Coordinates from that article (40 45 24 N, 73 55 29 W), correcting a pin some 1.9 km off in the research pool. The four features run across 1934 and 1935; month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Paramount moves him to its Astoria studio in Queens and he makes four pictures there with Le Pera: Cuesta abajo, El tango en Broadway, El dia que me quieras and Tango Bar. The four are made one after another across 1934 and 1935. He broadcasts on NBC as well, in a city that has no tango of its own and buys the records anyway. In a studio on Thirty-fifth Avenue he sings Cuesta abajo, El dia que me quieras and Por una cabeza, songs about Buenos Aires, none of them made in it.
suggested_refs: Kaufman Astoria Studios, 35th Avenue, Queens, site of all four American Gardel features

segments.name: Medellin and the Long Way Home

stops.name: Medellin, the sentence about the heart and the soul
stops.date_confidence: The quote is attested verbatim in Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel', reported from the June 1935 issue of Caretas magazine of Antioquia, Colombia, and carries no footnote there; the Alvarez (1995) citation that the research pool attached to it belongs to the next sentence in that article and is not a source for this line. The month is attested, the day is not and defaults to 01. Pin is the canonical Medellin coordinate; Antioquia is the department and Medellin its capital, and Gardel died there on 24 June 1935, which is almost certainly the occasion of the interview.
stops.campa: The tour through the Caribbean and the Andes reaches Colombia, where the records have gone ahead of him and the cantinas already know the repertoire. A magazine in Antioquia prints a sentence from him about his heart, his soul, and the two countries that divide them between them. He has told the press he is Uruguayan, written and had witnessed that he is French, and sworn to a consul that he was born in a valley near Tacuarembo. This is the last statement he makes on the subject.
stops.quote: My heart is Argentine, but my soul is Uruguayan, because that is where I was born
stops.quote_source: Carlos Gardel, reported in Caretas magazine (Antioquia, Colombia), June 1935; given inline and uncited in Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel'
suggested_refs: Caretas magazine (Antioquia), June 1935
The Museo Casa Gardeliana, Carrera 45 no. 76-50, Manrique, Medellin, founded 1972 by Leonardo Nieto Jardon

stops.name: Olaya Herrera, two aircraft on one field
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel' and Wikipedia (English), 'Olaya Herrera Airport', the latter giving Gardel and sixteen others dead. Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Accidente aereo de Medellin' gives a total of seventeen dead, names the second aircraft as SCADTA's Ford 5-AT-D C-31 Manizales with seven aboard under pilot Hans Ulrich Thoms, gives Gardel's pilot as Ernesto Samper Mendoza, and lists the guitarist Jose Maria Aguilar Porras among the dead of the F-31.
stops.campa: The Ford Trimotor F-31 runs down the field at Olaya Herrera and strikes the SCADTA Ford standing on it. Both aircraft burn. Seventeen people die, among them Gardel, the lyricist Alfredo Le Pera, the guitarists Guillermo Barbieri, Angel Domingo Riverol and Jose Maria Aguilar Porras, and the pilot Ernesto Samper Mendoza. The news reaches Buenos Aires the same day and the city stops working. He is forty-four by the Toulouse register and forty-seven by the Tacuarembo declaration.
suggested_refs: The Olaya Herrera airfield, Medellin, and the SCADTA Ford 5-AT-D C-31 Manizales

stops.name: Montevideo, two days lying in state
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the route and month. Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel' gives the transport of the body through New York and Rio de Janeiro and the two days lying in state at Montevideo before burial, with the year only; the month here is an ordering device and nothing more. The article tags the repatriation account loosely, and no source consulted gives a date of arrival in any of the three cities.
stops.campa: The body travels home the long way, through New York and Rio de Janeiro, and lies in state for two days in Montevideo. Thousands file past it. The city that gave him a nationality on his word alone in 1920 keeps him for forty-eight hours before Buenos Aires gets him back, which is as near as the argument between the two republics ever comes to being settled by anything factual. What date the coffin reached any of the three cities, no source consulted gives.
suggested_refs: Press accounts of the repatriation of Gardel's remains through New York, Rio de Janeiro and Montevideo

stops.name: La Chacarita, the bronze with a cigarette in its hand
stops.date_confidence: The burial at La Chacarita is attested by both the English and Spanish Wikipedia articles on Gardel, which give the year only; the month above is an ordering device. The statue and the cigarette tradition are attested by the Buenos Aires city tourism board's page on the Cementerio de la Chacarita, which does not name the sculptor or the date of erection: that is an open gap. The handwritten will produced by Armando Defino after the death is attested by Wikipedia (English), 'Carlos Gardel'.
stops.campa: He is buried at La Chacarita. His legal representative Armando Defino then produces a handwritten will in which Gardel states that he was born in Toulouse, France, so the dispute the funeral might have closed opens again over the coffin. Over the grave stands a life-size bronze of him smiling in a suit, left hand in the trouser pocket, right hand bent at the waist. Visitors put lit cigarettes between the bronze fingers and have never stopped, so the statue is almost always smoking.
suggested_refs: The Gardel tomb at the Cementerio de la Chacarita, sculptor and date of erection unrecorded in the sources consulted
The handwritten will produced by Armando Defino, 1935
sources: Buenos Aires city tourism board, turismo.buenosaires.gob.ar, 'Cementerio de la Chacarita'

stops.name: Abasto, the house opens with the papers inside it
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the day by Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Museo Casa Carlos Gardel', which also gives the 1997 declaration as a National Historical Monument, the donation to the city by Eduardo Eurnekian in 2000, and the display of authenticated copies of the Toulouse birth certificate and the handwritten will. A separate claim that UNESCO registered Gardel's recorded voice in its Memory of the World programme in 2003 appears in Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Carlos Gardel' but could not be verified against UNESCO itself, so no clustering of the two events is asserted here.
stops.campa: The house at Jean Jaures 735 opens as a museum. It was declared a national historical monument in 1997 and handed to the city by Eduardo Eurnekian in 2000, and among the objects displayed inside are authenticated copies of the Toulouse birth certificate and of the handwritten will. The two documents that say France now sit in the Abasto, three blocks from the cafe where he sang for market men, in a house that he bought for a laundress out of Toulouse.
suggested_refs: The Museo Casa Carlos Gardel, Jean Jaures 735, Abasto, opened 4 March 2003
